citation: Wayne A. Larsen, Alvin C. Rencher and Tim Layton, "Who Wrote the Book of Mormon? An Analysis of Wordprints", BYU Studies 20, no. 3 (1980): 225-251
claim: The book's 24 narrators and quoted speakers differ in their unconscious function-word habits, so it had many authors, and none of its passages resembles Joseph Smith, Cowdery, Rigdon, Spalding, Pratt or Phelps.
their_method: Function words (38 frequent, 42 infrequent; headline MANOVA on the 10 most frequent, arcsine-transformed rates) in about 1,000-word blocks of 24 speakers (251 blocks); MANOVA, cluster and discriminant analysis; 90 comparison blocks from eight nineteenth-century sources. Reported odds of a single author under 1 in 100 billion (p. 232).
replicable_with: The 1830 text, speaker labels for every quoted segment (they published only word counts per speaker), the candidates' writings, their word list (Appendix C).
replication_note: Rebuilt their speaker labelling with a model (simulated; 16 of their 24 speaker word counts within 10%) and ran their analysis: 17 speakers differ, Wilks' lambda 0.079, p = 8e-38; 4 of 215 speaker blocks classified to a nineteenth-century candidate. Both headline findings return (paper/replication-report.md section 1).
strengths: Published word list and method; first large stylometric study of the book; both findings reproduce from a fresh labelling of the 1830 text.
weaknesses: Blocks from one book are not independent random samples, so the p-value overstates certainty by an unknown amount; differences between speakers can track genre (sermon, war story, prophecy) rather than hands; candidate set closed and small.
our_approach: The finished study's pre-registered test (6.3) asked whether narrators separate as well as known different authors do (benchmark 0.96), and whether dictation order separates the chunks as well.
our_result: Narrators separate above chance (0.744 against 0.277) but below the 0.96 accuracy of distinct real authors, and dictation order separates the same chunks about as well (0.758). Claim c08 verdict: contradicted by its pre-written rule (docs/claims-verdicts.md).
what_holds: Holds in part: speakers do differ in function words, but no more than one writer's changing order or genre would explain, so the many-authors reading does not hold by the study's benchmark.
todo: Read Hilton 1990's redesign of this study and rerun its version too.

their_method: Five vocabulary-richness measures (Honore's R, V2/V, Yule's K, Sichel's alpha and theta on nouns) on 14 prophet samples of about 10,000 words from a modern edited text, with Joseph Smith's personal writing, three Doctrine and Covenants samples, KJV Isaiah and the Book of Abraham; cluster analysis and principal components.

what_holds: Holds: the 'prophetic voice' split returns, and the lab shows it is ordinary for people who write in two registers, not peculiar to Joseph Smith.

citation: Matthew L. Jockers, Daniela M. Witten and Craig S. Criddle, "Reassessing Authorship of the Book of Mormon Using Delta and Nearest Shrunken Centroid Classification", Literary and Linguistic Computing 23, no. 4 (2008): 465-491
claim: Sidney Rigdon and Solomon Spalding wrote most of the book: Rigdon is first or second choice for most chapters.
their_method: 110 common words; Delta and nearest shrunken centroids (R pamr) over 239 chapters of the 1830 text with biblical passages left in; 217 known samples from Cowdery, Pratt, Rigdon (mostly his 1864 'Book of the Revelations'), Spalding, KJV Isaiah-Malachi, Barlow and Longfellow. Reported: Rigdon first or second for 197 of 239 chapters; NSC cross-validated error 8.8%.
replicable_with: Their deposited word counts (Stanford Digital Repository, CC BY 3.0), R pamr, the candidates' texts.
replication_note: On their deposited data the same 110 words come back and NSC's cross-validated error is 8.76% (theirs 8.8%), but their printed chapter counts do not: Rigdon first or second for 169 (theirs 197), and their own tool gives our counts. With our candidate texts the result changes: Pratt 193, Rigdon 29. Swapping their Rigdon samples for signed Rigdon print halves his count (169 to 92) (paper/replication-report.md section 3).
strengths: Data deposited openly; standard, well-documented classifiers; included controls.
weaknesses: Closed set: every chapter must go to a listed candidate, so it cannot say 'none of these'; Joseph Smith left out; Rigdon represented mostly by text written in 1864; quotation left in; printed table not reproducible from the deposit.
our_approach: Open-set methods that must pass a known-answer benchmark before naming anyone; candidate samples screened for Book of Mormon quotation; results reported across candidate-sample choices.
our_result: Claim c07 contradicted: neither Rigdon nor Spalding is supported under the pre-registered rule; the synthesis gives Spalding 0.085 among the primary candidates.
what_holds: Does not hold: the method reproduces, but the Rigdon result follows the texts chosen to stand for each man.

citation: G. Bruce Schaalje, Paul J. Fields, Matthew Roper and Gregory L. Snow, "Extended Nearest Shrunken Centroid Classification: A New Method for Open-Set Authorship Attribution of Texts of Varying Sizes", Literary and Linguistic Computing 26, no. 1 (2011): 71-88
claim: With 'none of the above' allowed, most chapters fit none of the nineteenth-century candidates, so the Jockers attribution fails.
their_method: Extended nearest shrunken centroids, an open-set version that can assign a chapter to an unobserved author; candidates as in Jockers plus Joseph Smith; reported 175 of 239 chapters to an unobserved author, 35 Isaiah, 17 Rigdon, 8 Smith.
replicable_with: Their code (in Funai 2010), the candidates' texts (they split Rigdon early and late; Joseph Smith from Jessee's holographs).
replication_note: The published method, ported from the authors' code and checked (BOM-57), on our candidate texts: 225 of 239 chapters to an unobserved author (theirs 175), 13 Isaiah (theirs 35). The conclusion returns; the per-chapter assignments and their candidate texts were not recovered (paper/replication-report.md section 4).
strengths: First open-set treatment; addresses the main flaw of closed-set attribution.
weaknesses: BOM-57 showed the 'none' answer moves with the length and kind of the candidate samples (false 'none' falls from 80% to 0% between 1,000- and 10,000-word samples), so the method tends to say 'none' when candidate text is short or of a different kind; published model understates variance about fourfold.
our_approach: Benchmark of every method on known authors before use; ENSC retired after it failed fresh authors (BOM-58).
our_result: Claim c09 supported by its rule, with the caveat that no method passed the open-set bar and Joseph Smith and Cowdery are untested by the synthesis (too little pre-1830 writing).
what_holds: Holds in part: no candidate is supported, but the method's 'none' is partly an artifact of sample size, so it is graded evidence, not proof of absence.

The KJV and 1832 History figures reproduce.
strengths: A precise, countable feature with a clear historical curve; the KJV and 1832 History figures reproduce.
weaknesses: Comparison set of five Bible-style texts; did not search all printed books of 1700-1830.

what_holds: Holds in part: the rate is rare after 1700 and absent from Joseph Smith's other texts, but one 1820s mock-scripture author did produce it.

citation: Vernal Holley, Book of Mormon Authorship: A Closer Look (Ogden, Utah, 1983; rev. 1989), place-name map
claim: About 29 Book of Mormon place names match towns around the Great Lakes (Angola, Alma, Oneida/Onidah, Lehigh/Lehi), so the names were drawn from Joseph Smith's surroundings.
their_method: Name-by-name pairing on a map (from secondary source: the wheatandtares summary and https://www.fairlatterdaysaints.org/answers/Book_of_Mormon_place_names_from_North_America).

weaknesses: No chance baseline; many towns named after 1829; loose spelling rules.

what_holds: Does not hold: Palmyra is an ordinary region; single pairs like Oneida/Onidah cannot be judged by counts.

their_method: Reading of direction and distance passages; travel times turned into 'units of standard distance'; ten points; Sorenson's and Hauck's models graded (from our redesign note, docs/research/2026-11-22-redesign-geography.md).
